lesson_title: The Earth Is Falling Right Now
hook_text: Right now, the Earth is falling towards the Sun at thirty kilometres a second. And it will keep missing it for billions of years.
clip_script: Swing a tennis ball on a string and let go. It does not keep circling; it flies off straight. The string was pulling it inward the whole time. Planets have no string. They have gravity, a pull between any two masses, stronger for big masses, weaker with distance. Isaac Newton imagined a cannon on a mountain. Fire slowly and the ball falls nearby. Fire at eight kilometres a second and the round Earth curves away beneath it as fast as it falls. It keeps falling and keeps missing. That is an orbit. The Earth is doing exactly this around the Sun, moving sideways at thirty kilometres a second while gravity pulls it inward. Closer planets feel a stronger pull and race faster: Mercury's year is 88 days, Neptune's is 165 years. And they all circle in one flat plane, because the Solar System began as a spinning cloud that flattened like pizza dough.
visual_style: A whiteboard learner swinging a ball on a string, then Newton's cannon on a mountain with trajectories curving further until one circles the Earth, then planets on a flat disc around the Sun.
pacing: A simple demo, a classic thought experiment, then a cosmic payoff.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and explain why the Moon never falls down.
